metadata.title: Claude, Investigation Open.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude decide when a workplace issue becomes a formal investigation when it picks up the investigation-open skill? Take the skill apart — one folder, one SKILL.md, a linear checklist read before Claude acts — and land the carry-out that a skill is a specification, not new judgment.

beats.narration_text: Liam, in for Bear. You'd guess a skill called investigation-open lets Claude decide when to open a matter. It doesn't. It hands Claude a checklist to run intake. Let's take it apart.

beats.narration_text: Hear "Claude has an investigation-open skill" and it sounds like the model itself is deciding when a workplace matter becomes an investigation. That's the natural read. It's also wrong — and the reason it's wrong reveals what a skill actually is.

Delete the skill's folder. The model itself doesn't change — same weights, same reasoning. What Claude loses isn't authority to investigate; it never had that. What it loses is one intake checklist. That's the whole diff.

Here's what a skill actually is. A folder with one file — SKILL.md. Investigation-open is exactly that: a single markdown file listing the intake steps in plain English. No code. No new judgment. Just a document Claude reads before it acts.

Claude reads that file top to bottom, then works each step in the order it's written. No branching. No shortcuts. Unless a step explicitly says branch, execution stays linear. That's a design choice — predictability over flexibility.

That makes a skill a specification, not new judgment. The payoff: same intake, every matter, every time — reproducible. The trade-off: anything the file doesn't cover, Claude has no special opinion about. Consistency in exchange for scope.

So investigation-open never handed Claude the power to decide when to investigate. What it guarantees is repetition: every time the skill runs, the same file gets read, the same matter gets opened, the same intake runs. Same routine, every time. That's the whole trick.

beats.narration_text: Which means watching Claude open a matter and complete intake proves the checklist ran — it doesn't prove the underlying issue was judged correctly. A checklist followed to the letter can still miss what it was never asked to check. And a matter left unopened proves only that no one triggered the skill, not that nothing's wrong.

A skill named investigation-open doesn't hand Claude authority — it hands Claude a checklist to read before it starts. Same matter opened. Same intake run. Everything outside those written steps is still your call to make.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into any frontier LLM — Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Pick one recurring record I open the same way every time — a support ticket, an incident report, a new client file. Write me a SKILL.md for it: plain language, ordered steps. Then read it back and walk me through exactly what you'll open and log, before you touch anything. Go deeper: once it drafts the SKILL.md, ask it to name every step that requires human judgment — and explain why the skill can't automate that step away.
